“Madame and Mademoiselle L’Espanaye were not killed by spirits. Those responsible were corporeal beings and departed by corporeal means. How, then? Happily, there is only one way to reason on this question, and it must bring us to a definite conclusion. Let us consider the possible exits one at a time. Plainly, when the party came up the stairs, the assassins were either in the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye was discovered or in the adjoining chamber. Our search for outlets is therefore confined to those two rooms. The police have exposed the floors, ceilings, and wall masonry in every direction. No concealed passage could have eluded their scrutiny. Nevertheless, unwilling to rely upon their eyes, I inspected the place with my own. There were, indeed, no hidden exits. The two doors opening into the passage were firmly locked, their keys on the inside. Consider next the chimneys. Though of the usual width for eight or ten feet above the fireplaces, neither could accommodate a large cat along its entire length. Escape by the means already considered being absolutely impossible, we are left with the windows. No one could have left through the front-room windows unseen by the people in the street. The murderers must consequently have used the windows of the rear chamber. Having reached this conclusion so unambiguously, we cannot, as reasoning men, dismiss it because it appears impossible. Our task is simply to demonstrate that these seeming ‘impossibilities’ are not, in fact, impossible.

“There are two windows in that room. Furniture obstructs neither the view nor the approach to one, which is entirely exposed. The lower part of the second is concealed by the head of the cumbersome bedstead pushed against it. The first was found fastened securely from inside and withstood the greatest efforts to lift it. A large hole had been bored with a gimlet into the left of its frame, and a particularly stout nail occupied it, driven nearly to its head. Inspection of the second window revealed a similar nail placed in precisely the same manner; energetic efforts to raise that sash were equally unsuccessful. The police felt completely assured that no escape had occurred in either direction. Removing the nails and opening the windows was therefore judged an unnecessary labor.

“My examination went rather further, for the reason I have just explained: I knew that it was here that every apparent impossibility must be shown to have no real existence.”

About ten minutes later, the tea bell rang. When Virginia failed to come downstairs, Mrs. Otis sent a footman to fetch her. He returned after a while and said he could find Miss Virginia nowhere. Since she usually went into the garden each evening to gather flowers for the dinner table, Mrs. Otis was not worried at first. But when six o’clock struck and Virginia still had not appeared, she became seriously anxious. She sent the boys outside to look, while she and Mr. Otis searched every room in the house. At half past six the boys returned without finding any sign of their sister. Everyone was now frantic and at a loss when Mr. Otis suddenly remembered that, a few days earlier, he had allowed a group of Roma travellers to camp in the park. He immediately left for Blackfell Hollow, where he knew their camp was, taking his eldest son and two farm workers. The young Duke of Cheshire, beside himself with worry, begged to come too, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing there might be a fight. When they arrived, however, the travellers had gone. Their departure had clearly been sudden: the fire was still burning, and plates lay on the grass. Mr. Otis sent Washington and the two men to search the district, hurried home, and telegraphed every police inspector in the county, asking them to watch for a little girl kidnapped by vagrants or Roma travellers. He then called for his horse. After insisting that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, he rode along the Ascot Road with a groom. He had scarcely travelled two miles when he heard someone galloping behind him. Looking back, he saw the little Duke approaching on his pony, bareheaded and flushed. “I’m terribly sorry, Mr. Otis,” the boy gasped, “but I can’t eat dinner while Virginia is missing. Please don’t be angry. If you had let us get engaged last year, none of this trouble would have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t!”

The Minister could not help smiling at the handsome young rascal and was deeply touched by his devotion to Virginia. Leaning down from his horse, he patted the boy’s shoulders affectionately. “Well, Cecil, if you won’t go home, I suppose you’ll have to come with me. But I must find you a hat when we reach Ascot.”

Watching him in such moods, I frequently pondered the ancient philosophy of the Bi-Part Soul, diverting myself with the notion of two Dupins—the inventive and the analytical.

Do not imagine, from these remarks, that I am recounting a mystery or composing a romance. The qualities I have described in the Frenchman arose merely from an overexcited, or possibly disordered, intellect. An example, however, will best illustrate the nature of his observations on these occasions.

One evening we were walking along a lengthy, filthy street near the Palais Royal. Both of us seemed absorbed in our thoughts, and for at least a quarter of an hour neither had uttered a word. Suddenly Dupin spoke:

“He is certainly a very small fellow, and would be better suited to the Théâtre des Variétés.”

“That is beyond dispute,” I answered without thinking. So lost was I in reflection that I did not immediately notice how extraordinarily his remark accorded with my thoughts. A moment later I collected myself and was profoundly astonished.

“Dupin,” I said seriously, “I cannot understand this. I confess myself amazed, and hardly able to trust my senses. How could you possibly know that I was thinking about ——?” I stopped there to establish beyond doubt whether he truly knew whom I had in mind.

“——Chantilly,” he supplied. “Why stop? You were observing to yourself that his little figure disqualified him for tragedy.”

That was precisely the subject occupying my mind. Chantilly, formerly a cobbler in the Rue St. Denis, had developed a mania for the stage. He had undertaken the part of Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy of that name, and his reward had been notorious public ridicule.

“For Heaven’s sake,” I cried, “explain the method—if there is a method—that has allowed you to penetrate my soul in this affair.” I was, in truth, even more shaken than I cared to admit.

“The fruit seller,” my friend answered, “led you to decide that the repairer of soles lacked the height required for Xerxes et id genus omne.”

“The fruit seller! You bewilder me. I know no fruit seller at all.”

“The fellow who collided with you as we turned into this street, perhaps fifteen minutes ago.”

I then recalled that a fruit seller with a great basket of apples balanced on his head had accidentally all but knocked me down when we left the Rue C—— for the street in which we now stood. What possible connection this had with Chantilly remained entirely beyond me.
